title: Complex verb complementation and meaning
objectives: Choose complements after persuade, suggest and make.
Distinguish the meanings of remember and stop patterns.
Form active and passive make constructions.

explanation.heading: Meaning and use
paragraphs: A verb complement is a structure that completes or develops the meaning of a verb. Different verbs allow different patterns: “She persuaded him to wait”, “She suggested waiting” and “She suggested that he wait”. Knowing the meaning of the first verb is not enough; a learner must also know which structures it permits.

Sometimes the same verb allows more than one complement with a change of meaning. “I remembered to lock the door” says that I did not forget the required action. “I remember locking the door” describes a memory of a previous action. The difference is semantic, not just a matter of form.

explanation.heading: Form
paragraphs: Persuade normally takes an object followed by a to-infinitive: “They persuaded us to stay.” Suggest can take an -ing clause or a that-clause: “They suggested leaving” and “They suggested that we leave”. The mandative subjunctive leave is one formal option; in British English, “that we should leave” is another. “They suggested us to leave” is not standard in this meaning.

Some verbs allow an object and a bare infinitive: “She made him apologise.” In the corresponding passive, the to-infinitive is normally used: “He was made to apologise.” Let ordinarily takes an object and a bare infinitive in the active: “They let us enter.” Passive alternatives often use allow: “We were allowed to enter.”

explanation.heading: Examples in context
paragraphs: Compare “She stopped speaking” with “She stopped to speak”. The first means that her speaking ended; the second means that she paused another activity in order to speak. “Try restarting the device” proposes an experiment; “try to restart the device” emphasises making an attempt. Context may make the practical difference small, but the forms direct attention differently.

“I regret telling her” expresses regret about a past disclosure. “We regret to inform you that the service is closed” is a formal formula for giving unwelcome information now. In both cases, the clause following regret contributes to the interpretation; do not assume that one form always refers to every past or future situation.

explanation.heading: Contrasts and common mistakes
paragraphs: Avoid adding to after active make: “The delay made us reconsider”, not “made us to reconsider”. In the passive, however, to is normally required: “We were made to reconsider.” The change in voice changes the complementation pattern.

Not every verb accepts the same transformation. Advise can take an object plus a to-infinitive, as in “They advised us to wait”, whereas suggest normally does not take that pattern. Consult examples in context when learning a new verb, and distinguish grammatical error from a grammatical alternative with a different meaning.

examples.note: Persuade takes an object and a to-infinitive.

examples.sentence: They suggested that we should leave.
examples.note: The should-clause is a common British mandative pattern.
Active make takes an object and a bare infinitive.
The passive normally uses a to-infinitive.

examples.sentence: I remembered to lock the door.
examples.note: The speaker did not forget the action.
The speaker recalls a previous action.

examples.sentence: She stopped to speak to a colleague.
examples.note: She paused another activity in order to speak.

common_errors.reason: Suggest does not normally take an object plus to-infinitive in this meaning.

common_errors.incorrect: The coach made us to practise.
common_errors.reason: Active make takes a bare infinitive after its object.
The passive normally uses a to-infinitive.

summary: Verb complementation depends on the particular verb and its meaning.
Some -ing and infinitive patterns produce different interpretations.
Active make and its passive use different infinitive patterns.

exercises.explanation: Persuade takes an object and a to-infinitive.

option_feedback.a: “They persuaded that us leave.” does not fit here. Persuade takes an object and a to-infinitive.
option_feedback.b: “They persuaded us to stay.” fits here. Persuade takes an object and a to-infinitive.
option_feedback.c: “They persuaded us staying to.” does not fit here. Persuade takes an object and a to-infinitive.
option_feedback.d: “They persuaded to us stay.” does not fit here. Persuade takes an object and a to-infinitive.

exercises.explanation: Suggest can take an -ing clause.

options.text: They suggested to us leaving to.

option_feedback.a: “They suggested us to leave.” does not fit here. Suggest can take an -ing clause.
option_feedback.b: “They suggested we to leaving.” does not fit here. Suggest can take an -ing clause.
option_feedback.c: “They suggested to us leaving to.” does not fit here. Suggest can take an -ing clause.
option_feedback.d: “They suggested leaving early.” fits here. Suggest can take an -ing clause.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says the speaker recalls an earlier action?
exercises.explanation: Remember plus -ing refers to a memory of an earlier action.

options.text: I remembered to lock the door.
I intend to lock the door.
I will remember to lock the door.

option_feedback.a: “I remember locking the door.” fits here. Remember plus -ing refers to a memory of an earlier action.
option_feedback.b: “I remembered to lock the door.” does not fit here. Remember plus -ing refers to a memory of an earlier action.
option_feedback.c: “I intend to lock the door.” does not fit here. Remember plus -ing refers to a memory of an earlier action.
option_feedback.d: “I will remember to lock the door.” does not fit here. Remember plus -ing refers to a memory of an earlier action.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence means she paused another activity in order to speak?
exercises.explanation: Stop plus a to-infinitive expresses the purpose of stopping here.

option_feedback.a: “She stopped speaking.” does not fit here. Stop plus a to-infinitive expresses the purpose of stopping here.
option_feedback.b: “She finished speaking.” does not fit here. Stop plus a to-infinitive expresses the purpose of stopping here.
option_feedback.c: “She stopped to speak.” fits here. Stop plus a to-infinitive expresses the purpose of stopping here.
option_feedback.d: “She continued speaking.” does not fit here. Stop plus a to-infinitive expresses the purpose of stopping here.

exercises.explanation: Active make takes an object and a bare infinitive.

options.text: The coach made us to practise.
The coach made us practising to.
The coach made to us practise.

option_feedback.a: “The coach made us to practise.” does not fit here. Active make takes an object and a bare infinitive.
option_feedback.b: “The coach made us practising to.” does not fit here. Active make takes an object and a bare infinitive.
option_feedback.c: “The coach made to us practise.” does not fit here. Active make takes an object and a bare infinitive.
option_feedback.d: “The coach made us practise.” fits here. Active make takes an object and a bare infinitive.

exercises.explanation: Passive be made normally takes a to-infinitive.

option_feedback.a: “We were made practise.” does not fit here. Passive be made normally takes a to-infinitive.
option_feedback.b: “We were made practising.” does not fit here. Passive be made normally takes a to-infinitive.
option_feedback.c: “We were made to practise.” fits here. Passive be made normally takes a to-infinitive.
option_feedback.d: “We were make to practise.” does not fit here. Passive be made normally takes a to-infinitive.

exercises.explanation: Try plus -ing can propose testing a method.

option_feedback.a: “Try restarting the device.” fits here. Try plus -ing can propose testing a method.
option_feedback.b: “Remember restarting the device.” does not fit here. Try plus -ing can propose testing a method.
option_feedback.c: “Stop restarting the device.” does not fit here. Try plus -ing can propose testing a method.
option_feedback.d: “Regret restarting the device.” does not fit here. Try plus -ing can propose testing a method.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is a formal formula introducing unwelcome information?
exercises.explanation: Regret to inform is a formal formula used when delivering unwelcome information.

options.text: We regret informing you last week.
We regret to inform you that the service is closed.
We remember informing you last week.

option_feedback.a: “We regret informing you last week.” does not fit here. Regret to inform is a formal formula used when delivering unwelcome information.
option_feedback.b: “We regret to inform you that the service is closed.” fits here. Regret to inform is a formal formula used when delivering unwelcome information.
option_feedback.c: “We enjoy informing you now.” does not fit here. Regret to inform is a formal formula used when delivering unwelcome information.
option_feedback.d: “We remember informing you last week.” does not fit here. Regret to inform is a formal formula used when delivering unwelcome information.
